messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Nurse
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Vignette:
Mele was 21 when she came for treatment, a young Pacific Islander woman working as a nurse and living with her boyfriend, carrying herself with the alertness of someone who expected danger to break through ordinary life without warning. In describing the event that divided her life into before and after, she kept stopping and starting, saying she knew exactly what had happened but could not find words that felt usable. What emerged over several sessions was that she had been in a combat setting where casualties were coming in under conditions of repeated threat. The part that stayed with her most vividly was not a single image she could narrate cleanly from beginning to end, but fragments bound to sound and body: the rising scream of sirens, the crack of loud blasts, the pounding in her own chest as she moved among the injured and waited for the next impact. Even in the room with her therapist, if she got close to describing it, her face tightened and her whole body seemed to brace. She would become flooded so quickly that she had to stop speaking, sometimes pressing a hand to her sternum as if she were back inside that moment.

In the months after returning home, those sensory fragments began to intrude into daily life with very little warning. Sirens were especially potent. If an ambulance passed while she was walking to her car after a hospital shift, she did not simply feel startled; for a few moments she was no longer fully in the present. Her body reacted as if the combat scene were happening again, and she would find herself turning sharply, scanning for where to move, where the threat was coming from, before realizing she was in the employee parking lot. Loud noises had a similar effect. A metal tray dropped at the nurses’ station or a sudden bang in a hallway could make her go rigid and then instantly furious, with a burst of anger that felt as immediate as fear. What frightened her boyfriend was how quickly she could snap at him afterward over something minor, while to Mele it felt as though her whole system had already been pushed past its limit.

Her own body had also become a trigger. If she noticed her heart racing—while climbing stairs at work, hurrying between patient rooms, or even laughing hard—she was pulled toward the same sense of emergency she had felt during combat. Because of that, she gradually stopped exercising. Before, she had used movement to manage stress, but now anything that made her pulse pound felt dangerous in a way she could not talk herself out of. She began taking elevators instead of stairs at the hospital and avoided workouts entirely. She also started pulling back from situations that might make her feel light or hopeful. If friends invited her out or her boyfriend suggested doing something fun together, she often found a reason not to go. It was hard to explain, but feeling good seemed precarious, almost wrong, as if letting herself relax would leave her exposed.

At work, her vigilance had become woven into every shift. As a nurse she was expected to move efficiently through a busy environment, but Mele was continuously tracking doors, noises, footsteps, and the position of other people in the room. She checked hallways before entering, noticed every alarm and overhead sound, and kept orienting herself to exits. Colleagues experienced her at times as tense and irritable. If someone approached her from behind or if the unit suddenly became loud, she could turn with a sharpness that seemed disproportionate to the situation. She knew this was happening and hated it, but she was certain she needed to keep scanning because not doing so felt unsafe.

When memories surfaced directly, the strongest feeling was often rage. She described being overtaken by intense anger when she remembered the event, an anger so powerful that it eclipsed language. She would start to recall a detail and then feel overwhelmed so completely that she had to shut the memory down. At home this meant going silent mid-conversation or leaving the room abruptly. With her boyfriend, the accumulation had been painful: fewer outings, more edge in her voice, more time spent watching windows and listening for sounds outside. He wanted to comfort her, but she often seemed unreachable once she was pulled into those moments.

By the time she sought help, Mele was exhausted by the effort of getting through each day while feeling constantly on guard. What finally pushed her to come in was a recent incident at the hospital when a sudden siren outside sent her into a vivid flashback in the middle of her shift, followed by such intense anger and disorientation that she had to step away from patient care. She said she was afraid of what would happen if she could not control those reactions, afraid of being trapped in memories she could not fully describe and of becoming someone perpetually braced for danger. At the same time, she still hoped for something simple and specific: to hear a siren and remain in the present, to feel her own heart race without panic, and to be able to be with the people she loved without always searching the room first.
